Every serious API will eventually tell you to sit down and be quiet.

Hammer GitHub, Stripe, or AWS a little too eagerly and your requests start bouncing back with a polite but firm 429.

I always found that fascinating, so let's build the thing that says no. 

By the end of this post we'll have designed a rate limiter that actually holds up when you put it in front of real traffic, and I promise to only make a reasonable number of bucket puns along the way.

A rate limiter does one job: it decides how many requests a client is allowed to make in a given window of time. 

It protects your system from getting flattened, and it keeps one greedy user from eating everyone else's lunch.

Simple idea. Surprisingly spicy implementation.

Let's build it up piece by piece, the way you'd actually reason through it in an interview or a design doc.


  
  
  First, what are we even building?


Before writing a single line, let's agree on what "good" looks like. 

Here's my wishlist:



Configurable limits. Something like "100 requests per minute per user." 
The rules should not be hardcoded, because free users and premium users deserve different amounts of pain.

Honest rejections. When someone goes over, we return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and include helpful headers telling them how many requests they have left and when the window resets. No mystery.

Barely-there latency. This check runs on every single request, so it has to be fast. 
Let's aim for under 3ms at P95. If your rate limiter is slow, congratulations, you built a second bottleneck.

Highly available and shared. Multiple servers need to agree on the same counts. 
More on why that word "shared" is doing a lot of heavy lifting later.


Cool. Now let's start naive and let reality punch us in the face a few times.


  
  
  Attempt 1: the fixed window counter


The simplest thing that could possibly work is fixed window counting. Chop time into neat one-minute slices. 

Give each user a counter. 

Every request bumps the counter by one. 

Hit the limit, get rejected, and the counter resets when the next window starts.



# user makes a request
count = get(user_id)          # how many so far this minute?
if count >= 100:
    reject()                  # 429, come back later
else:
    increment(user_id)
    allow()





Clean. Readable. You could explain it to a rubber duck. So where do we keep this counter?

  
  
  Where do we put the counter? (this trips people up)


Your first instinct might be the database. 

Please don't. 

We'd be adding a write to the database on every request, which means the thing we built to protect our system is now quietly overloading it. 

That is peak "I have brought peace, freedom, and a full table scan."



Okay, database is out. 

What about keeping counters in memory on the server? Blazing fast. Love it. 

Except it only works if you have exactly one server, and nobody runs one server. 

The moment you scale out, each box keeps its own private counter. 

A sneaky user sends 100 requests to Server A and 100 to Server B and walks away with 200 requests per minute while your limit says 100. Whoops.

What we actually want is somewhere that is memory-fast and shared across every server. 

That's Redis. It's an in-memory data store, it hands us atomic counter primitives like INCR, and it can expire keys automatically so windows reset on their own. 

This is why Redis shows up in basically every rate limiter design ever drawn on a whiteboard.

So far so good. Now let me ruin it.

  
  
  The fixed window flaw nobody warns you about


Fixed windows have a nasty edge case hiding right at the seams. 

Picture a limit of 100 requests per minute.

A user fires 100 requests in the last 10 seconds of one minute, then another 100 in the first 10 seconds of the next minute.

Each window is technically within the limit. Both are 100 or under. 

But zoom out and you'll see 200 requests in a 20 second span, which is very much not the spirit of "100 per minute."

This happens at every window boundary, and once someone notices the pattern, they will absolutely abuse it.



The counter has no memory across the boundary, so it cannot see the burst spanning two windows. 

We need an algorithm that thinks in terms of a smooth rate rather than hard resets.

  
  
  Attempt 2: the token bucket (our hero)


Enter the token bucket, the algorithm quietly powering the limits at places like AWS and Stripe. 

Here's the mental model, and yes, it is literally a bucket.

Imagine a bucket that holds tokens. Tokens drip in at a steady rate. Every request has to grab one token to pass. No tokens left? Request gets rejected. That's it.


# refill based on time passed since we last looked
elapsed = now - last_refill
tokens  = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refill_rate)
last_refill = now

if tokens >= 1:
    tokens -= 1
    allow()
else:
    reject()   # 429, and tell them when to retry





Here's the diagram version of that decision:



Watch how this fixes our boundary nightmare. 

Set the bucket capacity to 100 and the refill rate to 100 per minute. 

During quiet stretches, tokens pile up toward the cap. 

When a burst comes in, the user spends whatever tokens they've saved, but they can never outrun the refill rate over the long haul. 

No matter how they time things around a boundary, they cannot conjure tokens that were never added.

That's the whole trick, and it's genuinely elegant. Two knobs control everything:



Capacity decides how big a burst you tolerate.

Refill rate decides your sustained throughput.


Capacity 100 with a refill of 100 per minute means a user can fire up to 100 requests instantly if they've been idle, but long term they're pinned to 100 per minute. 

Bursty when it's calm, strict when it counts. Chef's kiss.

Are there other algorithms? Sure. Sliding window logs, sliding window counters, leaky buckets, they each solve the boundary problem their own way.

But token bucket hits the sweet spot between "simple enough to actually implement correctly" and "good enough for almost everyone."

For a deeper rabbit hole, the token bucket writeup on Wikipedia is a decent start.

  
  
  Okay, but where does the limiter live?


We've got the algorithm. Now, architecturally, where do we run it? Three options, each with a personality.



Client side. Put the logic in the client app. 
Fast, but hilariously naive. 
You cannot trust clients to enforce their own limits, because a motivated user will just edit the code or skip the check entirely. 
This is like asking people to fine themselves for speeding.

Server side. Bake it into your application code. 
You get full control over the algorithm and everything lives in one place.
The downside is your rate limiting logic gets tangled up with business logic, and every service ends up reinventing the same wheel.

Middleware. A dedicated layer between clients and your APIs, like an API gateway, a reverse proxy, or a small custom service. 
Rate limiting stays cleanly separated from business logic, and you get one place to manage all your policies. 
The cost is a bit more moving parts in your system.


Which one wins? It genuinely depends. 

If you already run an API gateway doing auth, tucking rate limiting in there is a no-brainer. 

If you need some exotic custom algorithm, server side gives you room to move. 

But for most systems, middleware is the sweet spot: control and operational sanity without soldering the limiter to your business code.

Let's go with middleware and sketch the flow.

  
  
  The architecture, end to end


We'll store the rules ("premium gets 1000 per hour, free gets 100 per hour") in a configuration service. 

The middleware reads those rules, keeps token bucket state in Redis, and makes the call on every incoming request.



When a request lands, the middleware figures out who the user is, pulls their bucket from Redis, and checks for a spare token. 

Token available? Decrement it and pass the request along. 

Bucket empty? Return a 429 with a Retry-After header so the client knows exactly when to come knocking again. 

Be a good host. Tell your guests when the kitchen reopens xD

This is lovely for one rate limiting server. Then, as always, scaling shows up to spoil the party.

  
  
  Scaling breaks it: the race condition


Run multiple rate limiter instances against the same Redis and you can hit a classic race condition. 

Here's the exact sequence that loses a count:



Both servers read 3. Both decide the request is fine. 

Both write 4. We just quietly lost a count, and the counter now lies to us.

Do this enough times under load and your "100 per minute" limit turns into "somewhere around 100, we think, on a good day." 

Not exactly the airtight guarantee we promised.

The problem is that read, check, and write are three separate steps, and another server can sneak in between them.

  
  
  Atomic operations to the rescue


The fix is to make read plus check plus write a single indivisible operation, so nobody can wedge themselves in the middle. 

Redis lets us do this with Lua scripts, which run atomically on the server. 

The whole check-and-decrement happens as one unit, and the race condition simply cannot occur.


-- KEYS[1] = bucket key
-- ARGV[1] = capacity, ARGV[2] = refill_rate, ARGV[3] = now
local tokens = tonumber(redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) or ARGV[1])
if tokens >= 1 then
    redis.call("DECR", KEYS[1])
    return 1        -- allowed
else
    return 0        -- rejected, send a 429
end





(That snippet is simplified to keep the point front and center. A production version would compute the refill from elapsed time and store the last-refill timestamp too.)

Atomic operations turn our shaky-under-load counter into something you can actually trust across a fleet of servers. 

This is the difference between a rate limiter that works in the demo and one that works on Black Friday.

  
  
  Stuff I deliberately skipped (so we don't turn this into a book)


We covered the load-bearing bits, but a real production rate limiter opens up a bunch of fun follow-up questions worth chewing on:



Geographic latency. How do you handle a multi-region deployment where a global Redis is an ocean away?

Hot keys. What happens when a handful of users generate most of your traffic and hammer the same Redis key?

Hot reloading rules. How do you push new limits without restarting servers?

Fail open or fail closed? If Redis falls over, do you let everything through or block everything? Both answers can ruin your day, just differently.


Each of those is a great whiteboard prompt on its own, and honestly, "fail open vs fail closed" alone has sparked some very heated lunch debates.



  
  
  Wrapping up


So there's our bucket list, completed. 

We started with a naive counter, watched it leak requests at window boundaries, upgraded to a token bucket, argued about where to run it, moved the state into Redis so servers could agree, then made the whole thing atomic so scaling couldn't corrupt our counts.

That's the core of nearly every rate limiter you'll ever meet in the wild.

Next time an API hits you with a 429, you'll know there's a little bucket of tokens somewhere, freshly emptied, quietly telling you to hold your horses.

If you build one, or you have strong opinions on fail open vs fail closed, drop a comment. I'll try to reply before you hit my rate limit.

● Receiving course announcements and updates.
● Communicating with instructors and academic staff.
● Coordinating legitimate group projects.
● Receiving registration or scheduling information.
● Organizing academic correspondence.
Good email habits can make these interactions more effective. A useful academic email generally has a clear subject, a concise explanation, appropriate language, and enough context for the recipient to understand the request.
Students should also learn that different messages require different levels of urgency. An ordinary academic question may not require an immediate response, while a time-sensitive administrative notice may deserve prompt attention.
Academic Resources and Daily Organization

Depending on the institution, students may receive information concerning classes, examinations, libraries, student services, events, scholarships, career opportunities, and other academic activities.

● Receiving information about campus activities.
● Managing communication related to student services.
● Coordinating study groups.

 Use informative subject lines when sending academic email.
 Check the institutional inbox regularly.
 Archive messages that no longer require immediate attention.
 Use folders or labels for major courses and academic areas.
 Flag messages that require follow-up.

 Review important messages before deadlines.

Learning these features can help users handle large amounts of information efficiently. Search can help locate older messages, folders can separate major categories, and regular inbox maintenance can keep current tasks visible.
An email account may also serve as a central point for different areas of life. A user might receive personal correspondence, educational messages, professional communication, receipts, appointment notices, and service updates through the same address.
This makes email management an important digital-literacy skill. The ability to locate, classify, and prioritize digital information can be useful across many areas of modern life.
A “clean history” is therefore best understood as a clear and manageable record of legitimate communication rather than simply a measurement of account age.
Section 2: Practical Applications
Personal Communication
Yahoo Mail can support ordinary communication between individuals and organizations. People may use email to communicate with relatives, friends, community groups, schools, and service providers.
A well-managed mailbox makes these interactions easier to track because important correspondence remains accessible.
Real-life use cases include:
● Keeping correspondence with family and friends organized.
● Receiving appointment confirmations.
● Storing important receipts and records.
● Communicating with community organizations.
● Sharing documents and photographs.
Email can also provide a useful written record. When an arrangement is made through email, the relevant conversation can often be retrieved later if clarification is needed.
For example, a person organizing a community event may retain confirmation messages, schedules, and contact information in an appropriately labeled folder.
Education and Professional Organization
Email is also central to many academic and professional workflows. Students may receive course information, administrative announcements, and messages from instructors.
Professionals may use email for meetings, project discussions, document exchange, customer communication, and workplace coordination.
Practical applications include:
● Receiving academic or workplace announcements.
● Coordinating meetings and appointments.
● Communicating about projects.
● Maintaining records of important conversations.
● Managing documents and attachments.
An organized email system can reduce the amount of time spent searching for information.
Users can also connect email habits with calendars and task lists. When an important message contains a deadline or appointment, recording it separately can make it less likely to be forgotten.
Section 3: Educational Value & Skills
Managing a long-established Yahoo account can teach practical digital skills that extend beyond email.
One important learning outcome is information retrieval. Users learn to find historical messages using keywords, names, dates, subjects, or other search options provided by the service.
Another is organization. Folders and categories can help users distinguish between different areas of their lives.
Communication skills are equally important. Writing a clear email involves understanding the recipient, identifying the purpose, providing enough context, and avoiding unnecessary information.
Useful learning outcomes include:
● Digital organization.
● Email search skills.
● Professional writing.
● Time management.
● Information evaluation.
● Record keeping.
● Calendar coordination.
● File management.
● Task prioritization.
● Digital communication etiquette.
These skills can benefit students, employees, freelancers, parents, and retirees alike.
Life Skills Gained
Email management encourages responsibility and planning.
For example, receiving an appointment message is only the first step. A user must recognize the date, decide whether action is required, and record the information appropriately.
Likewise, receiving a work-related request may require prioritization, a response, and possibly a follow-up task.
These processes develop decision-making skills.
Email also teaches the importance of clear writing. A short message that explains its purpose clearly can often be more effective than a long message containing unnecessary information.
Users can also learn to manage attention. Constant notifications can interrupt work or study, so deciding when to check email is part of effective digital time management.
Section 4: Building Trust & Credibility
How Established Email Usage Can Support Credibility
A legitimately established email address can provide continuity. A person may use the same address for years when communicating with organizations, professional contacts, educational institutions, or personal connections.
This continuity can make communication convenient. Contacts do not need to learn a new address every time the person changes activities.
An established correspondence history can also help the account holder retrieve previous conversations when follow-up is necessary.
However, an old email account does not automatically establish credibility.
Credibility is based on communication quality, accuracy, reliability, and behavior. Someone with a newly created account can communicate professionally, while someone with an old account can communicate poorly.
Consistent Usage and Verified Information
Good communication habits are more important than account age.
Users should keep relevant information accurate and communicate through appropriate channels.
Key factors include:
● Accurate account information.
● Clear and respectful writing.
● Consistent use of an appropriate address.
● Timely responses when needed.
● Organized correspondence.
● Accurate attachments and documents.
● Appropriate communication etiquette.
A clean history can therefore be viewed as a record that is useful and understandable.
The objective should be to maintain legitimate communication that can be referenced when necessary.
Users should also distinguish between information they know and information they have merely heard. Developing this habit can improve the quality of communication and reduce misunderstandings.
Section 5: Productivity & Workflow
A long-established Yahoo mailbox can contain a significant amount of information. Without an organization system, users may spend unnecessary time searching through messages.
A productive workflow starts by identifying the main categories of communication.
Possible categories include personal correspondence, education, work, appointments, community activities, receipts, and records.
Users can then develop a simple organization system that matches their needs.
Actionable tips include:


 Check email at planned times.
 Use clear subject lines when writing messages.
 Organize important messages into appropriate folders.
 Archive completed correspondence where supported.
 Use search tools instead of manually scrolling through old messages.
 Mark messages requiring follow-up.
 Transfer important dates into a calendar.
 Review subscriptions periodically.
 Keep important documents easy to locate.
Periodically review and simplify the inbox.
Daily Email Routine
A simple daily routine can begin with a short review of incoming messages.
Users can identify which messages require immediate attention, which require a response later, and which are informational.
During focused work or study, it may be helpful to reduce unnecessary interruptions from notifications.
A second email review later in the day can address messages that arrived while the user was busy.
The appropriate routine depends on the individual. A professional who relies on email for customer communication may need frequent monitoring, while someone who primarily uses email for personal correspondence may need only one or two daily checks.
Weekly Organization
A weekly review can help maintain a clean and manageable history.
Users can look for unanswered messages, incomplete tasks, important upcoming dates, and documents that need to be organized.
This process prevents small administrative tasks from accumulating.
The goal is not to achieve a perfectly empty inbox. The goal is to make important information visible and easy to retrieve.
A practical system that is consistently maintained is usually more valuable than a complicated system that is rarely used.
Section 6: Case Studies / Examples
Example 1: A Student Managing Years of Academic Correspondence
A university student has used one legitimate Yahoo address for several years. The mailbox contains course announcements, messages from instructors, administrative notices, and correspondence about extracurricular activities.
When the student needs an old document, they initially search manually through many messages.
The student begins using search terms and organizes important academic correspondence into clear categories.
Later, when reviewing an old course requirement, the student can find the relevant message much more quickly.
Learning point: Search and organization skills become increasingly valuable as digital history grows.
Example 2: A Freelancer Managing Multiple Projects
A freelancer communicates with several clients through one Yahoo mailbox.
Each project generates messages containing schedules, questions, revisions, and documents.
The freelancer creates a straightforward folder structure and reviews outstanding correspondence at the beginning and end of each workday.
This allows the freelancer to identify unfinished conversations and locate previous project information quickly.
Learning point: Email organization can reduce administrative workload and support better project coordination.
Example 3: A Household Managing Everyday Records
A household receives email confirmations for appointments, school activities, community events, and other administrative matters.
One family member establishes a routine for reviewing messages and recording important dates in a calendar.
Messages that may be needed later are organized for easier retrieval.
Over time, household planning becomes easier because important information is no longer scattered across an unmanaged inbox.
Learning point: Email organization is useful for ordinary household administration as well as professional activities.
Example 4: A Professional Improving Email Writing
An employee notices that colleagues often need clarification after receiving their emails.
The employee changes their writing approach. Each message begins with a clear purpose, includes only necessary background information, and ends with a specific request or next step.
The employee also checks recipients and attachments before sending messages.
Communication becomes more efficient because recipients understand what is needed without repeated clarification.
Learning point: Managing an email account effectively includes improving the quality of outgoing communication, not only organizing incoming messages.
Section 7: Step-by-Step Guide
Define Your Main Email Purposes
Begin by identifying how you use Yahoo Mail.
Your account may support personal communication, education, work, appointments, community involvement, or a combination of these activities.
Understanding your main purposes helps you decide what information deserves priority.
If one account serves several areas of life, a small number of categories can help separate them.
Manage Your Own Legitimate Account
Use Yahoo's official account-management and account-creation procedures.
Your email account should be maintained by its rightful user and used appropriately.
Developing your own legitimate history gives you control over your communication records and allows your organizational habits to evolve naturally.
The objective should be long-term usefulness rather than simply accumulating account age.
Identify Important Categories
Review the types of messages already in your mailbox.
You might identify categories such as:
● Work.
● Education.
● Personal.
● Appointments.
● Receipts.
● Community.
● Travel.
● Documents.
Choose categories that reflect your real needs.
Avoid creating too many folders. Excessive organization can become difficult to maintain.
Practice Search and Retrieval
Learn how to find old messages efficiently.
Search for a particular sender, phrase, subject, date, or other distinctive information.
Practice locating several older messages so that you understand how the search system works.
This skill can save considerable time when you need information from an established email history.
Establish a Review Schedule
Choose one or more times during the day to review email.
During each session, identify messages requiring action, respond where appropriate, record important dates, and organize information that may be needed later.
Avoid assuming that every message requires an immediate response.
Prioritization is essential.
Review and Improve
At the end of each week, review your email habits.
Ask yourself:
● Can I find important messages quickly?
● Are my folders useful?
● Am I missing important correspondence?
● Are notifications interrupting my work?
● Do I have a reliable method for remembering deadlines?
● Are unnecessary messages creating clutter?
Make small adjustments based on your answers.
Over time, consistent habits can turn an established Yahoo mailbox into a practical archive for communication, planning, and record keeping.
Section 8: FAQs
What is an old Yahoo account?
An old Yahoo account is generally an account that has been legitimately active for an extended period. It may contain years of emails, contacts, documents, and other correspondence.
What does a clean Yahoo account history mean?
From an educational perspective, a clean history means that legitimate correspondence is organized and manageable. Important messages can be located, completed conversations can be archived, and unnecessary clutter can be controlled.
Does account age automatically create credibility?
No. Account age is not a substitute for professional communication or accurate information. Credibility develops through reliable behavior, appropriate communication, and consistent use.
Why can old email history be useful?
Historical messages can help users retrieve previous conversations, confirmations, documents, appointment information, and other records.
How can I organize a large Yahoo mailbox?
Start with a small number of useful categories, learn the available search tools, organize important messages, and establish regular review periods.
Can email management improve everyday skills?
Yes. Managing email can develop writing, organization, prioritization, record keeping, time management, and digital communication skills.
Resources such as usasvcit can provide general information and guidance about digital productivity. For current Yahoo features and account-management information, users should consult Yahoo's official resources.
Conclusion
Understanding old Yahoo accounts with clean history is most useful when viewed as an educational topic about legitimate digital communication, information organization, and everyday productivity.
An established Yahoo account can contain years of correspondence and records. That information may become valuable when users need to retrieve an old message, confirm an appointment, find a document, or review a previous conversation.
However, account age alone does not determine usefulness or credibility. The real value of an established email account comes from meaningful use, organization, accurate information, and consistent communication habits.
Managing a long-term inbox can also teach important life skills. Users learn how to prioritize information, write clearly, search historical records, maintain useful documents, coordinate schedules, and manage digital distractions.
These skills extend beyond email. Students can apply them to academic platforms, while professionals can use them for workplace communication and project management. Families can apply them to household administration, appointments, and community activities.
The most useful approach is therefore to build and manage your own legitimate email history rather than treating account age as the main objective.
An organized email account can function as a searchable archive, communication center, record-keeping tool, and productivity resource.
Educational resources such as usasvcit may provide general information and guidance. For current Yahoo features, account procedures, and service information, users should consult Yahoo's official documentation.
With consistent practice, effective email management can make digital communication easier, more organized, and more productive.
Call to Action
Start improving your email habits today by reviewing your current Yahoo mailbox and identifying the types of information you receive most often.
Create a simple organizational structure, learn how to search historical messages, schedule regular inbox reviews, and use a calendar or task system for important deadlines.
Focus on developing your own legitimate digital history through genuine communication and responsible account management.
Practice writing concise messages, checking information before sending it, organizing important records, and protecting your attention from unnecessary notifications.
Use educational resources such as usasvcit for general guidance and consult Yahoo's official resources for current account and feature information.
The long-term benefit is not simply having an old email account. It is developing digital habits that make communication, organization, planning, and everyday life more efficient.

content:
The gap between academic work and professional work is real, and you only feel it once you've crossed it. School optimizes for correct answers; industry optimizes for shipped outcomes alongside other people, on someone else's timeline, to someone else's standard. My first internship — four months of UI/UX and front-end work at LayOver — was where I first felt that shift, and I marked the moment it closed out in this reflection.


  
  
  The first real engagement changes how you work


The first time your work has to hold up in a professional setting, a few things become concrete that were abstract before. Code isn't graded and forgotten — it's used, maintained, and depended on by teammates. "Done" stops meaning "it runs on my machine" and starts meaning "it's ready for other people to build on."

Four months of front-end and UI/UX work taught me that professionalism is largely about consistency and reliability: showing up to a standard every day, communicating clearly, and delivering work that fits into a larger whole rather than standing alone.


  
  
  What the first professional engagement teaches




You're building for a team, not a grade. The measure of good work becomes whether it serves the people and product around it — which raises the bar on clarity and maintainability.

Craft and communication travel together. UI/UX work in particular made clear that building the thing and explaining the thinking behind it are two halves of the same job.

Reliability is the real reputation. In a professional setting, being someone whose work can be counted on matters more than any single impressive output.



  
  
  The takeaway


The first internship is where the transition from student to professional actually happens — where you learn that engineering is a team sport played to a standard, not a solo exam. Closing out those four months of front-end and design work at LayOver was a small milestone, but the working habits it built are the durable part.

content:
What Does NLP Mean?


Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the field focused on making computers work with human language. "Natural language" means how people actually speak and write—not programming languages or rigid commands, but everyday words, questions, and even mistakes.

NLP includes a wide range of computer tasks: recognizing spoken words, figuring out what a sentence means, translating between languages, or even generating new sentences from scratch. When you use a search engine, chat with a support bot, or let your phone autocomplete a message, you're using systems powered by NLP.

The goal is clear: enable computers to process and use human language to accomplish tasks that matter in the real world.


  
  
  Why Does NLP Matter to Engineers?


Most software serves people. People prefer to express themselves in their own words, not in dropdown menus or strict commands. Meanwhile, companies collect huge amounts of unstructured text: emails, reviews, customer chats, support tickets, documents, tweets, and more.

NLP bridges the gap between this messy text and the rigid world of code:



Chatbots for support: Answer user questions automatically.

Spam filters: Detect and block junk emails based on their wording.

Product feedback analysis: Summarize thousands of customer reviews into trends or highlights.

Search engines: Take human questions and match them to relevant documents or data.

Voice assistants: Turn spoken words into actions or responses.


Wherever software meets human language, NLP brings structure and automation.


  
  
  Human Language vs. Computer Data


Human language is unpredictable. Words often have multiple meanings (“bank” can refer to either a financial institution or the edge of a river). Context influences meaning. People skip words (“Lunch?”), use sarcasm (“Great job…”), invent slang, and regularly break grammar rules.

Computers, in contrast, are precise. In code and databases, data has a fixed structure: integers, true or false values, lists, or clear file formats like XML or JSON. There isn’t much room for ambiguity.

Teaching computers to deal with the ambiguity and quirks of human language is a fundamentally different challenge than, for example, sorting numbers in a database.


  
  
  Common NLP Tasks


Some everyday, practical problems that NLP solves:



Text Classification: Decide if an email is spam, a news article is about sports, or a tweet is positive or negative.



Example: Tagging a review as a “complaint” or “praise.”



Sentiment Analysis: Figure out if text expresses positive, negative, or neutral emotions.



Example: Detecting that “I love this phone” reflects a positive sentiment.



Named Entity Recognition (NER): Find the names of people, places, or organizations in text.



Example: In “Apple is opening a new store in San Francisco,” picking out “Apple” and “San Francisco.”



Machine Translation: Convert text from one language to another.



Example: Turning “hello, world” in English into “hola, mundo” in Spanish.



Question Answering: Read a set of documents and extract a direct answer to a user’s question.



Example: Given the text “The Eiffel Tower is in Paris” and the question “Where is the Eiffel Tower?”, the answer is “Paris.”




These cover the most frequent scenarios engineers run into, though NLP goes far beyond them.


  
  
  How NLP Works: The Big Picture


To a computer, language is just a series of characters. NLP starts by converting this text into a form a computer can process—usually by breaking it into words or sentences, and then mapping those words to numbers.

Once in this format, algorithms—ranging from simple rules to machine learning models—analyze the data. They might classify the text, summarize it, pull out information, or perform translation.

The final step is to transform the output of the algorithms (often just a number, or a list of numbers) back into something meaningful for humans: a label, an answer, or a readable text snippet.


  
  
  A ‘Hello, NLP’ Code Example


Let’s walk through a minimal example: counting how often each word appears in a piece of text. This task is called a “word frequency count.” It’s a basic, but essential, step in many NLP workflows.

Here’s how you would do it in Python:



text = "Hello world! This is the world of NLP. Hello again, world."
# Convert to lowercase for consistent counting
text = text.lower()

# Remove punctuation (here, just periods and exclamation marks for simplicity)
for char in ['.', '!', ',']:
    text = text.replace(char, '')

# Split the string into words
words = text.split()

# Count word frequencies
freq = {}
for word in words:
    if word in freq:
        freq[word] += 1
    else:
        freq[word] = 1

print(freq)






This script:


Makes all letters lowercase so “Hello” and “hello” are treated the same.
Removes basic punctuation.
Splits the cleaned text into separate words.
Counts how many times each word appears.


The output looks like this:



{'hello': 2, 'world': 3, 'this': 1, 'is': 1, 'the': 1, 'of': 1, 'nlp': 1, 'again': 1}






Word counts are basic, but powerful. They’re used to rank search results, bring up relevant suggestions in apps, and even help flag suspicious emails in spam filters. Most advanced NLP systems still start with this fundamental step: treating language as data, then building on top of that structure.





  
  
  Key Takeaways



NLP enables computers to process and understand human language.
Human language is ambiguous and unstructured compared to computer data.
Key NLP tasks include classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation.
Practical NLP applications power chatbots, search engines, and spam filters.
A simple word frequency count is a foundational NLP technique.



  
  
  Try It Yourself


Write a Python function that takes a short sentence and returns a list of its unique words, ignoring case and punctuation. Test your function with three different sentences to verify it handles each correctly. Consider edge cases such as repeated words and basic punctuation marks.

content:
Hello, I'm Shrijith Venkatramana. I'm building git-lrc, an AI code reviewer that runs on every commit. Star Us to help devs discover the project. Do give it a try and share your feedback for improving the product.




There is a strange fact at the heart of modern AI:

If you make a language model bigger, give it more data, and spend more compute training it, its performance improves according to remarkably predictable mathematical relationships.

This was not obvious in 2019.

At the time, it was reasonable to think that neural networks might eventually hit some messy combination of architectural limitations, optimization failures, or diminishing returns. Instead, Jared Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI found something much more interesting: over enormous ranges of model sizes, datasets, and compute budgets, language-model loss followed approximate power laws.

That observation became one of the intellectual foundations of the modern LLM industry.

It also led to one of the great practical mistakes of early LLM scaling.

OpenAI's 2020 work suggested that, given a fixed compute budget, you should spend disproportionately on larger models and relatively little on data. Two years later, DeepMind's Chinchilla experiments showed that this allocation was badly wrong: many famous models were simply too large and insufficiently trained.

For developers, scaling laws are more than an interesting piece of ML history. They explain why model providers obsess over parameters, tokens, GPUs, and training runs—and why the economics of inference can completely change what "the best model" means.

Let's work from intuition to the math.


  
  
  1. The basic idea: intelligence has a surprisingly smooth price curve


Imagine training models with:


100 million parameters
1 billion parameters
10 billion parameters
100 billion parameters


You might expect their performance to jump around unpredictably.

Instead, something closer to this happens:



Model size          Loss
-----------         ----
100M                 3.8
1B                   3.1
10B                  2.6
100B                 2.2





The improvements get smaller, but they do not suddenly disappear.

The important observation is that the relationship is approximately a power law:


Loss ~= constant + A / N^alpha





where:


N     = number of model parameters
alpha = scaling exponent





The exponent is small.

That is crucial.

If:


alpha = 0.08





then multiplying the model size by 10 gives:


improvement factor = 10^0.08 ~= 1.20





That sounds unimpressive.

But now multiply the model by 100:


100^0.08 ~= 1.45





And by 1,000:


1000^0.08 ~= 1.74





The returns diminish, but they remain remarkably persistent.

This is why "just make the model bigger" worked for so long.

Kaplan, McCandlish, Henighan and their OpenAI colleagues measured these relationships across models and training regimes spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. Their 2020 paper found that loss scaled predictably with three quantities:


model size,
dataset size,
compute used for training.


That was the important discovery.

The question then became:

If compute is limited, where should you spend it?

  
  
  2. A little history: how GPT-3 turned scaling into an engineering strategy


The story becomes more interesting when you look at what happened around the research.

In the late 2010s, OpenAI had already demonstrated the usefulness of Transformer language models. GPT-2, released in 2019, had 1.5 billion parameters.

Then came GPT-3.

The 2020 GPT-3 paper described a 175-billion-parameter model—more than 100 times larger than GPT-2.

That sounds absurd if you think about models as software projects.

But scaling laws provided a rationale:


If loss continues following a predictable curve as model size increases, then increasing model size is not merely making the model "larger." It is buying measurable improvements.


This changed the engineering question.

Instead of:


"What clever architecture should we invent?"





you could increasingly ask:


"How much improvement do we get for another $10M of compute?"





That is a radically different research program.

And it is why the modern LLM race became so capital-intensive.

The underlying model is relatively simple:


more parameters
       |
       v
more computation
       |
       v
lower training loss
       |
       v
better downstream capability





The first three arrows are where scaling laws are strongest.

The last arrow is messier.

That distinction matters.

  
  
  3. The Kaplan equations: three things you can scale


Kaplan et al. essentially studied three independent axes.

Let:


N = number of parameters
D = number of training tokens
C = training compute
L = validation loss





A simplified version of the relationships looks like:


L(N) ~= L_inf + A / N^alpha_N

L(D) ~= L_inf + B / D^alpha_D

L(C) ~= L_inf + E / C^alpha_C





The exact fitted constants aren't the interesting part.

The shape is.

  
  
  Scaling model size




L(N) ~= L_inf + A N^(-alpha_N)





Increasing N reduces loss.

But each additional increase buys less than the previous one.

  
  
  Scaling data


Similarly:


L(D) ~= L_inf + B D^(-alpha_D)





More training tokens improve the model.

Again, diminishing returns.

  
  
  Scaling compute


Compute roughly captures the interaction between the two:


C ~= k N D





for dense Transformer training, because each token requires work proportional to the number of parameters.

This is the first really useful equation for a developer:


training compute ~= parameters x training tokens





More precisely, the FLOP count has architecture-dependent constants, but the approximation is excellent for intuition.

Suppose you have:


N = 10B parameters
D = 300B tokens





Then the basic scaling quantity is:


N x D = 3 x 10^21





You cannot escape this multiplication.

A 10x larger model trained on the same amount of data costs roughly 10x as much compute.

A model of the same size trained on 10x more tokens also costs roughly 10x as much.

So now we have an optimization problem:


Given fixed C:

How should I divide C between
model size N and data D?





This is where Kaplan's work became operationally important.

  
  
  4. The surprising Kaplan result: make the model very large


Kaplan et al. estimated that compute-optimal training favored increasing model size aggressively.

In simplified terms, their results suggested relationships roughly like:


N_opt ~= C^0.73

D_opt ~= C^0.27





The exact fitted exponents depend on the formulation and regime, but the qualitative result was striking:

As your compute budget increases, model size should grow much faster than the number of training tokens.

Why?

Because a larger model was substantially more sample-efficient.

Imagine you have a fixed $100M compute budget.

You could choose:


Small model + enormous dataset





or:


Large model + smaller dataset





Kaplan's measurements suggested the second option would give better loss.

That thinking was highly influential.

It helps explain the era of enormous models:


GPT-3       175B
Gopher      280B
MT-NLG      530B





The industry was effectively following the logic:


compute is scarce
        |
        v
make the model very large
        |
        v
models become increasingly capable





And for a while, this looked like the correct recipe.

Then DeepMind did something rather inconvenient.

  
  
  5. Chinchilla: the industry discovered it had been starving its models


In 2022, Jordan Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind published Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.

They trained more than 400 models ranging from roughly 70 million to over 16 billion parameters, using datasets ranging from 5 billion to 500+ billion tokens.

Their conclusion was almost the inverse of the prevailing practice:

Large language models were being trained on far too little data.

They found that, under their compute-optimal regime, model size and training tokens should scale approximately together:


N doubles
    |
    v
D should roughly double





The famous practical rule became approximately:


~20 training tokens per parameter





for the regime studied by Chinchilla.

The experiment that made this famous was Chinchilla itself.

DeepMind trained:


Gopher:
280B parameters
~300B tokens

Chinchilla:
70B parameters
~1.4T tokens





Chinchilla had one quarter as many parameters but roughly four times as much training data, while using approximately the same training compute.

And it performed substantially better across a broad collection of evaluations.

This was a beautiful example of why scaling laws matter.

The question wasn't:


"Which model is bigger?"





It was:


"Which allocation of compute produces the most capable model?"





Those are very different questions.

  
  
  A back-of-the-envelope example


Suppose you have:


C = fixed compute budget





Consider two hypothetical models.

Model A:


N = 100B
D = 1T tokens





Model B:


N = 50B
D = 2T tokens





Ignoring architecture-specific constants:


C_A ~= 100B x 1T
C_B ~= 50B x 2T





Therefore:


C_A ~= C_B





Same rough training compute.

But Model B has twice as many training tokens per parameter.

If you are in the undertrained regime, that can produce a much better model.

This was Chinchilla's central lesson.

  
  
  6. The economics: training-optimal isn't necessarily deployment-optimal


Here is where things get particularly interesting for developers.

Suppose two models have comparable quality:


Model A: 400B parameters
Model B: 100B parameters





If Model B required more training data to achieve that quality, you might still prefer it.

Why?

Inference.

Every generated token requires the model's weights to participate in computation.

For a dense Transformer, inference cost is approximately proportional to:


parameters x generated tokens





at a high level.

So if:


Model A = 400B
Model B = 100B





then, all else equal:


Inference compute A
------------------- ~= 4
Inference compute B





That difference becomes enormous at scale.

Suppose your product generates:


1 billion tokens/month





A 4x difference in inference compute is no longer an academic detail.

It affects:


GPU count
latency
electricity
cooling
datacenter capacity
API margins
price per token
maximum concurrent users


And this exposes an important limitation of Chinchilla-style scaling.

Training-optimal is not necessarily business-optimal.

If you are training a model once and serving it for billions of requests, paying somewhat more during training to obtain a smaller model can be economically rational.

Later research explicitly incorporated inference demand into scaling-law optimization and found that sufficiently high inference workloads can favor models smaller than the standard Chinchilla-optimal solution.

Think of it as an amortization problem:


Total cost
=
training cost
+
(number of inference tokens x cost/token)





For a research model used 10,000 times:


training cost dominates





For a model used by hundreds of millions of people:


inference cost dominates





The optimal model can therefore change dramatically.

This is why "the best model" is an incomplete engineering concept.

There is:


best model for training compute
best model for latency
best model for inference cost
best model for quality
best model for a fixed hardware budget
best model for a business with 1B requests





Scaling laws give you the machinery for thinking about those tradeoffs.

  
  
  7. What developers should actually take away


You probably aren't going to train a 500-billion-parameter model in your garage.

So why should you care?

Because scaling laws teach a much more general engineering lesson:

LLM performance is often governed by smooth resource tradeoffs rather than isolated architectural breakthroughs.

When evaluating a model, ask three questions.

  
  
  1. How much model capacity am I buying?




N = parameters





More parameters generally provide more capacity, with diminishing returns.

But parameter count alone is increasingly misleading because architectures such as MoE can have huge total parameter counts while activating only a subset per token.

  
  
  2. How much information has the model actually seen?




D = training tokens





A 100B model trained on 1T tokens and a 100B model trained on 10T tokens are very different objects.

Parameter count without training-token count tells you surprisingly little about how well-trained a model is.

  
  
  3. What is my compute budget?


Training:


C_train ~= N x D





Inference:


C_infer ~= N x generated_tokens





These two equations are enough to explain a surprising amount of the economics of LLMs.

And they give you a useful mental model when reading model announcements.

If someone announces:


"New 500B parameter model!"





your immediate questions should be:


How many tokens was it trained on?

How much compute was used?

How many parameters are active per token?

What is the inference cost?

What quality does it achieve per dollar?





The headline parameter count is only one coordinate in a much larger optimization problem.

  
  
  Conclusion: scaling turned AI into an industrial science


Kaplan's 2020 paper was important because it suggested that LLM progress wasn't just a sequence of lucky architectural discoveries.

There was a measurable curve.

Make the model larger:


loss falls





Give it more data:


loss falls





Give it more compute:


loss falls





And, remarkably, these improvements often followed power laws over huge ranges.

Then Chinchilla demonstrated the other half of the story:


You don't merely want a large model.

You want the right model for your compute budget.





That distinction transformed the field.

The interesting question today isn't simply:


"How big can we make the model?"


It is:


"Given a fixed amount of silicon, data, money, energy, and inference demand, what allocation produces the most useful intelligence?"


That is a much more interesting engineering problem.

And it is one reason scaling laws are worth understanding even if you never train an LLM yourself.

If you had $10 million to build an LLM today, would you spend it on a larger model, more training data, better data quality, or cheaper inference—and why?

Computer-using agents, or CUAs, treat the monitor like a human operator. Instead of hitting hidden APIs or raw HTML trees, these models ingest screenshot frames, turn visual state into intent, and execute clicks and keystrokes directly. They parse native desktop environments without caring about underlying markup shifts. When a button moves five pixels left, the model adapts visually instead of throwing an exception.

Architectural divergence between major lab offerings comes down to state and safety boundaries. One approach leans into deep native OS hooks and tight sandboxing for deterministic safety. The alternative optimizes for fluid multimodal reasoning over raw browser and desktop frames, letting workflows adapt faster across varied software stacks.

title: One Script, Five Signals: My Free Model Server Scorecard
title_hi: One Script, Five Signals: My Free Model Server Scorecard
summary:
A free model server looks like a gift. Until it returns garbage at 3 a.m.

Every week, a new model drops. Every week, so
content:
A free model server looks like a gift. Until it returns garbage at 3 a.m.

Every week, a new model drops. Every week, someone wires it into production on day one. That's how incidents start.

I've spent weeks probing free endpoints. Concurrency. Structured output. Time-of-day variance. The pattern never changes: free works, until it doesn't.

So I built a scorecard. One script. Five signals. Fifteen minutes. Here's the evaluation.

This week I pointed the harness at MonkeyCode's free tier. MonkeyCode is an open-source project. It ships with 10 million free tokens and a free server option. I wanted one answer: where does it hold up, and where does it break?

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.


  
  
  The five signals


A single benchmark run tells you almost nothing. Five signals, repeated three times, tell you a lot.



TTFT — time to first token. This is your perceived latency.

Output rate — words per second after the first token.

Error rate — HTTP 4xx, 5xx, timeouts, exceptions.

Output integrity — is the response complete and parseable?

Consistency — variance across repeated runs.


Why five signals? Because latency alone lies. A server can answer fast and still be broken. It can answer slowly and still be fine. The combination tells the real story.

One good run proves nothing. Three runs show a pattern. That's the whole trick.


  
  
  The experiment design


Fixed prompts. Fixed order. Fixed client. No retries.

Retries hide failures. I want the raw failure. So the harness records everything and retries nothing.


Five tasks: summarize, code, JSON, Q&A, rewrite.
Three repetitions per task. Fifteen calls total.
One machine. One network. One time window.
Every result lands in a JSON array.


Why fifteen calls? Enough to expose gross failures. Small enough to run during a coffee break.


  
  
  The script


Here's the whole harness. It targets any OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint.



# scorecard.py — 15-minute free model server evaluation
import json, os, statistics, time
import httpx

BASE_URL = os.environ["MC_BASE_URL"]   # e.g. https://host/v1
API_KEY = os.environ["MC_API_KEY"]
MODEL = os.environ["MC_MODEL"]

PROMPTS = {
    "summarize": "Summarize eventual consistency in three bullets.",
    "code": "Write a Python retry helper with exponential backoff.",
    "json": 'Return JSON only: {"name": "Ada", "role": "engineer"}',
    "qa": "What is idempotency? Answer in one short paragraph.",
    "rewrite": "Rewrite 'utilize' as 'use' in one short sentence.",
}

def run_one(task, prompt):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    first_token = None
    text = ""
    try:
        with httpx.stream(
            "POST", f"{BASE_URL}/chat/completions",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"},
            json={"model": MODEL,
                  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
                  "stream": True},
            timeout=60.0,
        ) as r:
            if r.status_code != 200:
                return {"task": task, "error": f"HTTP {r.status_code}"}
            for line in r.iter_lines():
                if not line or not line.startswith("data:"):
                    continue
                data = json.loads(line[5:])
                delta = data["choices"][0]["delta"].get("content", "")
                if delta:
                    if first_token is None:
                        first_token = time.perf_counter() - t0
                    text += delta
    except Exception as exc:
        return {"task": task, "error": type(exc).__name__}

    total = time.perf_counter() - t0
    words = len(text.split())
    return {
        "task": task,
        "ttft_s": round(first_token, 2) if first_token else None,
        "total_s": round(total, 2),
        "words": words,
        "words_per_s": round(words / max(total - (first_token or 0), 0.01), 1),
    }

def summarize(results):
    clean = [r for r in results if "error" not in r]
    return {
        "calls": len(results),
        "errors": len(results) - len(clean),
        "median_ttft_s": round(statistics.median(r["ttft_s"] for r in clean), 2),
        "median_words_per_s": round(statistics.median(r["words_per_s"] for r in clean), 1),
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    results = [run_one(t, p) for t, p in PROMPTS.items() for _ in range(3)]
    print(json.dumps({"runs": results, "score": summarize(results)}, indent=2))






Run it:



export MC_BASE_URL="https://your-endpoint/v1"
export MC_API_KEY="your-key"
export MC_MODEL="the-model-name"
python scorecard.py






Output looks like this (illustrative — your numbers will differ):



{
  "runs": [
    {"task": "summarize", "ttft_s": 1.8, "total_s": 9.4, "words": 82, "words_per_s": 10.7}
  ],
  "score": {"calls": 15, "errors": 0, "median_ttft_s": 1.9, "median_words_per_s": 11.2}
}






Word count is a proxy. Stream chunks are not tokens. If the endpoint returns usage fields, prefer those.


  
  
  How to read the scorecard


Thresholds are workload decisions. Here are mine.




Signal
Pass
Warn
Fail




TTFT median
< 2 s
2–5 s
> 5 s


Output rate
> 20 w/s
5–20 w/s
< 5 w/s


Error rate
0%
< 20%
≥ 20%


Integrity
all clean
one bad
many bad


Consistency
p95 < 2× median
< 3×
≥ 3×




Take a hypothetical run. Median TTFT of 1.8 s is a Pass. Median output rate of 11 w/s is a Warn. Zero errors is a Pass. That's one Warn. Yellow flag. Proceed with caution.

A "Fail" in any row is a red flag. Two "Warn" rows are a yellow flag. Everything else is a maybe.

Free tiers don't come with SLAs. The scorecard is your SLA.


  
  
  Where free model servers break


I've seen the same failure modes across several free endpoints.



Silent truncation. HTTP 200 with an empty or half-finished body. The worst one, because logs look clean.

Burst rate limits. 429s appear only under load. My earlier concurrency probe on a comparable free server broke at 16 parallel calls.

Cold starts. The first call after idle is painfully slow. The second is fine.

Degraded output. The server stays up, but the quality drops. No error. No warning.



  
  
  How to confirm silent truncation


Silent truncation hides behind HTTP 200. Here's the check.


Compare the response length against what the prompt asked for.
Look for an unfinished final sentence. A missing period is a tell.
Re-run the same prompt. Repeated truncation is a server bug, not a fluke.


The scorecard catches all four modes. That's why error rate and integrity are separate signals.


  
  
  What I concluded


The conclusion is the method, not my numbers.

One window of fifteen calls proves nothing permanent. It proves the server can survive fifteen calls. That's it. Run the scorecard twice, on different days. If both runs pass, you have a usable free tier. If not, you have evidence. That's more than most teams have.

What surprised me? Nothing. Free infrastructure behaves like free infrastructure: generous at the start, vague at the edges. The scorecard turns vague into concrete. That's the value.


  
  
  When to use a free model server


Use it for:


Prototypes and internal demos.
Batch jobs with retries and a dead-letter queue.
Drafting, summarization, classification — where a bad output is cheap.
Testing your own client code against a real endpoint.


Don't use it for:


User-facing latency with a contract.
Regulated or sensitive data. Free tiers carry no guarantees.
Anything where a silent empty 200 is worse than a loud error.


The rule is simple: match the workload to the guarantee. Free tiers guarantee nothing. So give them nothing critical.


  
  
  Extending the harness


Fifteen calls is the floor, not the ceiling. Add what your workload needs.


Larger prompts. Feed it a 2,000-word document.
Longer streams. Ask for 500 words and watch the tail.
Different hours. Run the same script at 9 a.m. and 9 p.m.
Concurrent calls. My earlier probe showed concurrency is where free servers die first.


Keep the scoring logic identical. That's how you compare runs honestly.


  
  
  Limitations of this evaluation


The harness is small by design. Fifteen calls catch gross failures. They don't prove reliability.


One client, one region, one time window.
Word rate is a proxy, not token throughput.
Free tiers change. Re-run the scorecard before you trust it.



  
  
  Try it


The script is the deliverable. Point it at any endpoint.

If you want a first target, MonkeyCode's free tier and free server option are a reasonable place to start. The project is open source, so the client code is inspectable.

Run the scorecard twice. Then decide. That's the whole evaluation.

  Introduction


Analizamos cómo el uso de AI en la codificación afecta a los desarrolladores. Exploramos su dependencia, beneficios y desafíos.


  
  
  ¿Qué es la codificación por AI y cómo funciona?


La codificación por AI se refiere al uso de algoritmos y modelos de aprendizaje automático para ayudar en la escritura de código. La encuesta reciente de Coddy revela que un sorprendente 80% de los desarrolladores sienten que su relación con la AI es más adictiva que beneficiosa. Esto plantea preguntas sobre la naturaleza de la dependencia tecnológica y su impacto en el desarrollo.

Los sistemas de codificación AI utilizan técnicas como el procesamiento del lenguaje natural (NLP) para interpretar y generar código. Por ejemplo, herramientas como GitHub Copilot funcionan alimentando modelos de lenguaje con grandes volúmenes de código existente para aprender patrones y estilos de programación.


  
  
  Mecanismos y Arquitectura




Modelos de Lenguaje: Algoritmos como GPT-3 son entrenados en vastas bases de datos de código y documentación.

Integración en IDEs: Muchas herramientas AI se integran directamente en entornos de desarrollo como Visual Studio Code, ofreciendo sugerencias en tiempo real.


[INTERNAL:analisis-tecnologico|Comparativa entre herramientas de codificación AI]

La importancia de entender estos mecanismos radica en que, a medida que más desarrolladores adoptan estas tecnologías, se vuelve esencial evaluar sus efectos en la productividad y creatividad.


  
  
  Impacto Real en el Desarrollo Web


La dependencia de herramientas AI plantea desafíos únicos para los equipos de desarrollo. Uno de los problemas más destacados es que, aunque estas herramientas pueden acelerar ciertas tareas, también pueden llevar a una menor comprensión del código generado.


  
  
  Consecuencias a Largo Plazo




Despersonalización del Código: Los desarrolladores pueden perder la habilidad de escribir código limpio y optimizado si dependen demasiado de las sugerencias automatizadas.

Problemas de Mantenimiento: La falta de comprensión del código generado puede resultar en un mayor tiempo dedicado a solucionar errores más adelante.



  
  
  Comparaciones con Tecnologías Alternativas



En lugar de depender exclusivamente de AI, algunos equipos están volviendo a métodos tradicionales como la revisión por pares y el uso de frameworks más claros y documentados. Esto asegura que todos los miembros del equipo comprendan el código, independientemente de si fue generado automáticamente o manualmente.


[INTERNAL:mejores-practicas|Estrategias para evitar la dependencia del AI]


  
  
  Casos Reales


Empresas como GitHub y Facebook han implementado herramientas AI en sus flujos de trabajo, observando tanto aumentos en la velocidad del desarrollo como desafíos en la calidad del código.


  
  
  ¿Cuándo se debe usar la codificación por AI?


La integración de AI en el desarrollo no es un enfoque único. Aquí hay algunas pautas sobre cuándo podría ser apropiado utilizar estas herramientas:


  
  
  Usos Específicos




Proyectos Prototipos: Cuando se busca rapidez para validar ideas iniciales, la AI puede ser útil para generar código básico rápidamente.

Automatización de Tareas Repetitivas: Para tareas que son monótonas y no requieren creatividad, como la generación de boilerplate code.

Aumentar Eficiencia: En situaciones donde se necesita refactorizar grandes secciones de código, las herramientas AI pueden ayudar a encontrar soluciones rápidas.


Sin embargo, es crucial ser consciente de sus limitaciones y no depender completamente de ellas para decisiones críticas.


  
  
  ¿Dónde se aplica esta tecnología?


El uso de codificación por AI se extiende a múltiples industrias. Sin embargo, su efectividad puede variar significativamente según el contexto:


  
  
  Aplicaciones por Industria




Tecnología: Empresas como Google están utilizando AI para optimizar procesos internos y mejorar productos.

Finanzas: En el sector financiero, la AI ayuda a automatizar informes y análisis complejos.

Salud: Herramientas que generan registros médicos o ayudan en diagnósticos también están comenzando a incorporar capacidades de codificación por AI.


[INTERNAL:casos-exito|Ejemplos específicos en diferentes industrias]


  
  
  Desafíos Regionales


En Colombia y España, donde los ciclos tecnológicos pueden ser más conservadores, la adopción puede verse obstaculizada por problemas como infraestructura deficiente o falta de capacitación adecuada.


  
  
  ¿Qué significa para tu negocio?


Para empresas en Colombia, España y LATAM, entender el impacto del uso intensivo de AI es crucial:


  
  
  Implicaciones Locales




Costos Aumentados: La dependencia excesiva puede llevar a costos ocultos debido a errores generados por la falta de entendimiento del código.

Adopción Conservadora: Las empresas deben evaluar cuidadosamente cuándo adoptar herramientas AI, asegurándose de contar con personal capacitado para supervisar su uso.

Regulaciones Locales: Con el auge de la privacidad y regulaciones tecnológicas, las empresas deben asegurarse de que las herramientas que utilizan cumplan con las normativas locales.


Esto significa que las decisiones sobre tecnología deben ser informadas y estratégicas, considerando tanto los beneficios inmediatos como los riesgos a largo plazo.


  
  
  Conclusión + Pasos Siguientes


Para cualquier equipo que esté considerando integrar herramientas AI en su flujo de trabajo, aquí hay algunos pasos prácticos:


  
  
  Acciones Recomendadas




Evaluar Necesidades: Determina si realmente necesitas integrar una herramienta AI o si las soluciones existentes son suficientes.

Piloto Controlado: Si decides seguir adelante, implementa un piloto controlado con un grupo reducido para medir resultados sin comprometer todo el equipo.

Documentar Resultados: Asegúrate de documentar todas las interacciones con la herramienta AI para comprender su impacto real.

  ¿La codificación por AI reemplazará a los desarrolladores?


No necesariamente. Aunque puede aumentar la eficiencia, todavía se requiere supervisión humana para garantizar la calidad del código.

content:
Crumbongo started from a pretty stupid little question:

What if the number of accessible cookies on the website you're visiting could become game currency?

So I built it.

Crumbongo is a tiny local Chrome game where you choose a website, let the extension count the accessible cookie records for that site, and turn only that number into game rewards.

No cookie names or values are used for gameplay.


  
  
  From a tiny experiment to an actual little game


The first version was basically:


choose a website;
check its accessible cookie count;
harvest that number into a Cookie Jar;
spend the cookies on Bongo.


Then I kept building on top of it.

Crumbongo now has:


a level and progression system;
pixel-art cosmetics;
multiple habitats;
companions;
local statistics;
Monkey Climb;
Cookie Stack.


The whole thing still lives inside a Chrome extension popup.


  
  
  The technical side


Crumbongo is deliberately small.

There is no React, TypeScript, Vite, game engine, backend or framework involved.

It's built with:


vanilla JavaScript;
HTML;
CSS;
Chrome Extension APIs;

requestAnimationFrame for the minigames;

chrome.storage.local for persistent game progress.


The minigames are built with regular DOM elements and CSS rather than Canvas.

That constraint became part of the fun: figuring out how far I could push a tiny extension popup without turning the project into something much larger.


  
  
  Local by design


Because the core mechanic involves browser cookies, I wanted the privacy model to be extremely clear.

Crumbongo requests access one site at a time.

For gameplay it only uses the number of accessible cookie records returned for that site.

It does not:


store or transmit cookie names;
store or transmit cookie values;
modify or delete browser cookies;
use an account system;
use analytics or tracking;
send gameplay data to a backend.


Game progress stays locally in the browser.


  
  
  The game-design part became more interesting than I expected


Once I added progression, I realized the cookie mechanic could support much more than a simple counter.

Cookies became a resource.

The Cookie Jar became something you wanted to grow.

Levels started unlocking things.

Cosmetics gave the currency a purpose.

Habitats and companions made Bongo's world feel like it was expanding.

Then the minigames gave players another way to interact with the same economy.

One of the hardest parts wasn't implementing features. It was deciding when something technically worked but still didn't feel right.

For example, Cookie Stack originally allowed the tower to grow too tall. It worked perfectly from a programming perspective, but after actually playing it, the next catch became unfair.

So the tower now clears after five pieces.

Tiny adjustment, much better game.


  
  
  AI-assisted development


I also used AI tools during development, particularly Codex as a coding assistant and generative tools for parts of the visual exploration.

My workflow wasn't "prompt -> finished game".

It was usually:

define a specific change -> implement -> test manually -> inspect screenshots -> adjust -> repeat

AI was extremely useful for implementation speed, but decisions about progression, balance, visual positioning, what to remove, and whether something actually felt good still came from repeatedly using the game.

That part ended up being one of my favorite lessons from the project.


  
  
  Is the mechanic actually unique?


As far as I could find while researching it, I couldn't find another game built around this exact mechanic:

using the accessible cookie count of the website you're currently visiting as the resource that powers a game.

If someone knows of one, I'd genuinely love to see it.


  
  
  Try Crumbongo


Crumbongo is free on the Chrome Web Store:

https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/crumbongo/glnecpfjdlljaihbnmaijkaldfbhalfj

Official website:

https://crumbongo.teobella.com/

I'm especially curious about one thing:

When you first see Crumbongo, does the core cookie-count mechanic make sense immediately?

And if you try it, I'd love to know what feels confusing, unnecessary, frustrating, or missing.

title_hi: I’ve spent the last few years deeply embedded in Web3: running operations, building products, and pitching to VCs. Here's how i pick a dev team:
summary: The single biggest operational risk for early-stage founders remains hiring traditional hourly dev shops. Before partner
content:
The single biggest operational risk for early-stage founders remains hiring traditional hourly dev shops. Before partnering with any external dev team, I've learned to run them through this 5-point evaluation framework:

The 5-Point Evaluation (co-founder approved)

1. Quality of Questions

If a team asks zero questions, it’s an immediate red flag. It's impossible to deeply understand a project without asking anything. But quality matters. Weak devs ask easily googled questions about basic blockchain mechanics. Strong engineers ask highly specific questions focused entirely on your business logic, edge cases, and tokenomics.

2. Proposing Solutions, Not Problems (obvious one)

A weak team will message you saying, "We have a problem, how should we fix it?" A mature team says, "We hit a blocker. Here are three architectural workarounds, the trade-offs for each, and our recommendation."

3. Deep Ecosystem Knowledge

Coding isn't enough. If an agency claims they can build a top-tier lending protocol but doesn't understand the role of risk engines and oracles, they are tourists. Your developers need to know top-tier market leaders like Gauntlet, Steakhouse, Chaos Labs, and RedStone, and understand how their risk modeling and data feeds directly dictate market parameters. If they lack this context, their expertise is strictly surface-level.

4. Full Product Lifecycle Understanding

Writing code and calling it a day is a massive mistake. A real partner understands what happens outside the IDE. They account for security audit buffers, integration with risk providers and oracles before mainnet, and the proper setup of on-chain governance and admin functions.

5. High Agency & Proactivity

Elite teams care about your overall success, not just their Jira tickets. To quote a BD i work closely with:

“When a client is about to make a massive mistake, you have two choices: stay silent and watch them fail, or step in with your expertise, even uninvited, and say: 'We hear what you want to do, but here’s a better way so you don't globally screw this up.'”
Teams for 2026

You can try start with:

DeFi Wonderland — Best for Core DeFi & Governance

Consensys — Best for Enterprise Ethereum & Ecosystem Tooling

Woof Software — Best for Fixed-Outcome & High-Agency Architecture

LimeChain — Best for ZK & Custom DLT Solutions

For transparency, you can recommend your own or don’t recommend at all. But, I'd rather hear real founder experiences than pick someone arbitrarily to just fill the list. Anyway, I hope these practical tips help.
To sum up

In Web3, your dev team is your biggest operational risk. And honestly, don't let the quiet market stop you. It’s not just about the potential ROI it’s about actually laying the bricks for the next chapter of the web, that’s how I see it.

title: The blog that invented its own infrastructure
